stem: A law firm's Amazon S3 bucket has a bucket policy that denies every s3:DeleteObject and s3:PutObject call from any principal, yet objects keep transitioning to S3 Glacier Deep Archive and expiring on schedule exactly as an existing S3 Lifecycle rule defines. Why does the Lifecycle rule keep running despite the deny-all bucket policy?

choices.text: The bucket policy's deny statements only apply to requests made outside business hours
Lifecycle actions are performed by the S3 service itself and are not evaluated against the bucket policy the way a principal's request is

An S3 Lifecycle rule is configured once at the bucket level and therefore always overrides any bucket policy statement that its scheduled transition or expiration actions would otherwise conflict with
The deny statement has no effect because it was written after the Lifecycle rule was created

rationale: S3 Lifecycle transition and expiration actions are carried out by the S3 service itself against the object, and they are not evaluated against the bucket policy the way an external principal's request would be, which is exactly why a deny-all bucket policy does not stop them. Nothing in the scenario mentions time-of-day restrictions, and bucket policy deny statements are not limited to business hours by default. Framing this as the Lifecycle rule "overriding" the bucket policy is not accurate; the two are simply evaluated through different paths, not in a policy-priority contest. The order in which a policy statement and a Lifecycle rule were created has no bearing on whether either one applies.
